Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 40-year-old woman with past childhood asthma and hay fever presents with 48-hour wheeze and dyspnoea starting after dust exposure; nocturnal worsening; no chest pain, dizziness, or infection symptoms; has rescue inhaler but has not used it.

Working diagnosis  
• Acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by dust/allergen exposure.

Differential diagnoses consistent with transcript  
• Allergic lower-airway reaction to dust mites (Medium likelihood).  
• Viral upper/lower respiratory tract infection with reactive airway component (Medium-Low likelihood).

Plan (per consultation)  
• Advise patient to attend local GP/clinic same day for objective assessment (oxygen saturation check, peak flow, possible spirometry).  
• Consider trial of antihistamine (OTC) en route or at clinic if allergy suspected.  
• Possible prescription of oral steroids after in-person assessment if asthma confirmed.  
• Clinician to send summary letter to patient’s GP via app.  
• Educate on prompt use of reliever inhaler if symptoms worsen while awaiting review.  
• Safety-net: seek urgent care if breathing deteriorates, unable to speak in full sentences, or develops chest pain.

Management Plan

- Immediate: Attend GP/urgent care today for assessment including pulse oximetry and peak-flow; obtain OTC antihistamine if available.  
- Medications: May restart/use salbutamol inhaler as needed; oral corticosteroids to be considered by GP.  
- Follow-up: GP review expected to take ~10 minutes; further management guided by objective findings.  
- Patient education: Recognise red-flag asthma symptoms; ensure reliever inhaler in date; consider regular preventer discussion at follow-up.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Asthma exacerbation (High) – Past asthma, classic wheeze, nocturnal symptoms, clear dust trigger.  
2. Acute allergic reaction / dust-mite hypersensitivity (Moderate) – Immediate dust exposure and hay fever history; less likely due to persistent worsening.  
3. Viral upper or lower respiratory tract infection (Low–Moderate) – Possible trigger of wheeze but lacks cough, fever, or URI signs.
